items.prompt: A CLI command receives `AccessDenied`, but the engineer believes the configured profile has the required role. Which first diagnostic action identifies the principal that actually signed the request?
constraints: The CLI can call STS with the current credentials.
The engineer has multiple profiles configured.
No policy change has yet been justified.

options.text: Run `sts get-caller-identity` with the same profile and environment to confirm the account and principal ARN in use.
Attach administrator access to every configured profile so the engineer can compare them.
Change the S3 bucket policy before confirming which principal made the request.
Use the root user's ARN as the expected caller because all CLI profiles resolve to root.

feedback.Reason: Confirming the actual caller prevents policy changes for an identity that did not make the failing request.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: STS `GetCallerIdentity` returns the account and identity information associated with the credentials used for the call and does not require permission for the operation itself.
Details.scenarioApplication: The engineer should run it with the same profile, environment variables, and role session path as the failing command, then compare the returned ARN with the policy principal.
Details.errorCorrection: Broadening every profile or editing a resource policy before confirming the caller hides the credential-selection defect.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The check identifies the principal but does not prove that all downstream policies allow the target action; those layers remain part of the next diagnostic step.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Broadening permissions is unsafe and does not establish which credentials the failing command used.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Changing the bucket policy for an unconfirmed principal can grant the wrong identity access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CLI profiles do not resolve automatically to the root user.

items.prompt: A deployment pipeline assumes a role successfully, but the role's policy was updated in account A while the pipeline's ARN points to the same role name in account B. What should the architect verify?
constraints: Both accounts contain a role with the same name.
The pipeline can assume either role depending on the configured ARN.
The requested resource exists only in account A.

options.text: Verify the full target role ARN and the account in the assumed-role session before changing either policy.
Add `*` resources to both roles because same-name roles are always interchangeable.
Delete the role in account B so STS will redirect the request to account A.
Use the account root password in the pipeline to remove account ambiguity.

feedback.Reason: An IAM role ARN includes its account, so identical role names in different accounts are distinct authorization principals.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: STS assumes the exact role ARN supplied by the caller. The resulting session's account and role identity determine which identity policy, trust relationship, and organization controls apply.
Details.scenarioApplication: The pipeline should use the intended account-A role ARN and verify the returned assumed-role identity before modifying the policy.
Details.errorCorrection: Wildcard permissions and deleting a valid role are not substitutes for correcting the principal selection, and root credentials create a larger risk.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Explicit account-qualified ARNs make cross-account automation clearer; role names alone are insufficient for a multi-account diagnostic.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Broadening both roles increases access and does not identify which account the pipeline assumed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: STS does not redirect a role ARN to another account, and deleting the role is destructive.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root credentials do not solve account selection and should not be placed in a pipeline.

items.prompt: A developer may create a Lambda function and has permission to call `lambda:CreateFunction`, but the create request fails when it specifies an execution role. Which missing permission is most likely?
constraints: The execution role trust policy trusts Lambda.
The developer's Lambda action permission is correct.
The developer should pass only this one execution role.

options.text: Grant the developer a narrowly scoped `iam:PassRole` permission for the execution role, optionally constrained to the Lambda service.
Grant the developer `iam:CreateUser` because Lambda execution roles are IAM users.
Add the developer to the role trust policy so passing a role is the same as assuming it.
Grant `lambda:*` and `iam:*` on `*` so the service can choose any role.

feedback.Reason: Creating or updating an AWS resource that uses a role requires the caller to be allowed to pass that role to the service.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: `iam:PassRole` authorizes a principal to pass an IAM role to an AWS service for a resource or operation. It is distinct from assuming the role and should be scoped to the intended role and service.
Details.scenarioApplication: The developer can create the function only after receiving `iam:PassRole` for the Lambda execution role; the role's trust policy remains the service-assumption control.
Details.errorCorrection: An execution role is not an IAM user, and modifying trust or granting wildcards does not express the narrow pass-role requirement.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: PassRole is sensitive because it can delegate the role's permissions to a service; its resource and service conditions should be reviewed as carefully as the role policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Lambda execution roles are IAM roles, and creating an IAM user is unrelated to passing one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Trust controls who or what assumes the role; `iam:PassRole` controls the caller's delegation of the role to a service.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Wildcard permissions create unnecessary delegation authority and are not a diagnostic fix.

items.prompt: A deployment role can pass an application execution role to ECS but receives `AccessDenied` when passing a different administrative role. Both roles trust ECS. What is the narrowest diagnostic conclusion?
constraints: The caller has `iam:PassRole` only on the application role ARN.
The ECS service principal is valid in both target role trust policies.
The administrative role is not required by the application.

options.text: The caller's `iam:PassRole` resource scope excludes the administrative role; keep the application scope and do not grant the unused role.
Add the administrative role to the ECS trust policy because trust policies grant callers PassRole permission.
Grant `iam:PassRole` on `*` because all roles trusted by ECS have identical risk.
Delete the application role so the caller can pass the administrative role by elimination.

feedback.Reason: The failing role is outside the caller's PassRole resource scope; the correct response is to preserve the narrower delegation boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: `iam:PassRole` is evaluated against the role resource being passed. A role's trust policy does not grant the caller permission to pass it; the caller needs a matching identity-based allow.
Details.scenarioApplication: Because the application needs only the application role, no permission change is justified for the administrative role.
Details.errorCorrection: Granting PassRole on `*` would let the deployment role delegate arbitrary role permissions to ECS.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a legitimate new workload needs the administrative role, it should be reviewed as a new delegation requirement rather than silently broadening the existing deployment role.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Trust policies control who assumes the target role; they do not authorize the caller's PassRole API action.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Wildcard PassRole can delegate highly privileged roles and violates least privilege.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting a needed application role is destructive and does not repair authorization semantics.

items.prompt: A CI role can pass an application role to Lambda but should not pass it to EC2 or SageMaker. Which policy condition can narrow the delegation by service?
constraints: The same application role ARN is used for Lambda only.
The CI role already has the correct `iam:PassRole` action and resource.
The team wants AWS authorization, not a naming convention, to enforce the service boundary.

options.text: Add an `iam:PassedToService` condition that allows passing the role only to the Lambda service principal.
Put the Lambda service principal in the role permissions policy because permissions policies control who can pass roles.
Use the role description to record Lambda and rely on operators to follow it.
Grant `iam:PassRole` to the Lambda function so the function can enforce the CI role's delegation.

feedback.Reason: The `iam:PassedToService` condition constrains the service to which a role may be passed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM supports the `iam:PassedToService` condition key for `iam:PassRole`, allowing a caller's delegation to be constrained by the AWS service principal receiving the role.
Details.scenarioApplication: The CI policy can pass the application role to Lambda while rejecting attempts to use the same delegation for EC2 or SageMaker.
Details.errorCorrection: The target role's permissions policy does not decide who may call PassRole, and descriptions or function permissions are not request-time delegation controls.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The condition must match the service principal and the actual service integration; a condition that is too narrow can break a valid deployment and should be tested in the pipeline.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The role permissions policy controls what the service can do after assumption, not which caller may pass it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A description is documentation and cannot prevent an unauthorized service from receiving the role.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The Lambda function is not the principal making the CI PassRole request.

items.prompt: A Lambda function can be invoked, but its code receives `AccessDenied` when reading one DynamoDB table. The developer's invoke permission is correct. Which identity should the architect inspect?
constraints: The function executes successfully and reaches its handler.
The function has an execution role.
The caller invoking Lambda is not the identity performing the DynamoDB read.

options.text: Inspect the Lambda execution role's permissions policy and resource scope for the DynamoDB read action.
Add DynamoDB permissions to the developer who invoked Lambda because the caller's permissions flow into the function automatically.
Add the Lambda service principal to DynamoDB as a table item because service principals are data records.
Give the function the root access key because execution roles cannot authorize application code.

feedback.Reason: Code running inside a Lambda function uses the function's execution role for AWS API calls, not the invoker's identity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Lambda assumes the configured execution role and makes its temporary credentials available to the function runtime. The execution role permissions policy must allow the function's downstream actions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect should inspect the execution role's DynamoDB action and table ARN, while leaving the developer's invoke permission separate.
Details.errorCorrection: The invoking principal authorizes `lambda:InvokeFunction`; it does not automatically grant the function the invoker's downstream permissions, and root keys are unsafe.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The execution role should be scoped to the function's actual data access and monitored independently from the identities that deploy or invoke it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Lambda's downstream API calls use its execution role, not the invoker's permissions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A service principal belongs in an authorization relationship, not as a DynamoDB data record.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Lambda execution roles are the supported workload identity and should not be replaced by root keys.

items.prompt: An ECS task can pull its image and send logs, but the application inside the task receives `AccessDenied` when reading S3. Which role distinction should the architect check?
constraints: The ECS agent successfully pulled the image and configured logging.
The application uses the AWS SDK from inside the task.
The task definition specifies both an execution role and a task role.

options.text: Inspect the task role's permissions; the execution role covers ECS agent operations such as image pull and logging, not the application's AWS calls.
Add S3 permissions only to the execution role because every container call uses that role.
Add the ECS service principal to the S3 bucket as an object so the SDK can read it.
Use an access key baked into the container image because task roles cannot reach S3.

feedback.Reason: ECS separates the execution role used by the ECS agent from the task role used by application containers.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The ECS task role provides permissions for containers in the task to call AWS services. The task execution role is used by the ECS/Fargate agent for operations such as image pulls and log delivery.
Details.scenarioApplication: The task role must allow the required S3 action and bucket/object scope; changing only the execution role will not authorize the application SDK call.
Details.errorCorrection: The ECS service principal and task execution role serve different stages, and embedding a long-term access key in the image is unsafe.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate roles make the application and platform permissions easier to constrain, but both role paths must be included in an access-denied diagnosis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The execution role is for ECS agent operations; application containers use the task role.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A service principal is not an S3 object and does not provide the task's application authorization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Task roles are the supported workload identity and avoid distributing long-term keys in images.

items.prompt: A developer can call CloudFormation but a stack update fails when CloudFormation tries to create an IAM role. The stack uses a configured service role. Which authorization path should be inspected?
constraints: The developer's CloudFormation API request is accepted.
The stack service role is the identity CloudFormation uses for resource operations.
The service role trust policy already trusts CloudFormation.

options.text: Inspect the CloudFormation service role's permissions, including any `iam:PassRole` required for the role resource being created.
Add IAM permissions to the developer only because a service role never affects stack resource operations.
Grant the CloudFormation service role the root user's access key so it can create any resource.
Remove the service role so CloudFormation will use an anonymous principal for IAM operations.

feedback.Reason: When a CloudFormation service role is configured, its permissions govern stack resource operations, including role delegation requirements.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFormation can use a service role to make calls on behalf of the stack. The service role must trust CloudFormation and have the permissions needed for the template, including PassRole when a resource is passed to another service.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect should inspect the service role action/resource scope and the template's role relationships rather than broadening the developer's unrelated caller permissions.
Details.errorCorrection: The developer's ability to start the stack is distinct from the service role's ability to create resources, and root keys must not be supplied to services.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A service role creates a durable deployment authority that should be narrowly scoped and reviewed when templates change.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A configured service role performs the stack operations; developer permissions do not automatically flow into it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root keys are not service-role credentials and would create unrestricted long-term exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Removing the service role does not create a safe anonymous execution path and can change the stack authorization model unexpectedly.

items.prompt: An IAM role policy allows `kms:Decrypt` on a customer managed KMS key, but decrypt still fails. The key is correct and no SCP denies the request. Which additional authorization surface must be checked?
constraints: The role's identity policy contains the required action and key ARN.
The role is authenticated and the ciphertext uses the target key.
The key is a customer managed KMS key.

options.text: Inspect the KMS key policy and grants, because KMS authorization depends on the key policy or an equivalent enabled delegation path as well as IAM permissions.
Add S3 bucket permissions because KMS key policies are stored as S3 objects.
Replace the role with the account root user because IAM roles cannot use customer managed keys.
Remove encryption from the ciphertext so KMS no longer evaluates authorization.

feedback.Reason: KMS adds a key-policy authorization surface; an IAM allow alone does not make every customer managed key request succeed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS KMS evaluates key policies, IAM policies, grants, and other applicable controls to determine whether a principal can use a key. The key policy must enable the intended principal or delegation path for the IAM permission to be effective.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should inspect the key policy and grants for the role and action, then preserve the narrowly scoped IAM and key permissions.
Details.errorCorrection: KMS key policies are not S3 objects, root is not required for role-based decryption, and removing encryption is not a safe authorization fix.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Key policies are resource-owner controls and should be kept narrow; granting broad account permissions in a key policy can expand decryption authority.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: KMS key policies are evaluated by KMS and are not managed as S3 object permissions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM roles can use KMS keys when the key policy and IAM policy authorize the request.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Changing data protection to avoid a policy check creates a security regression rather than solving authorization.

items.prompt: A producer role in account A is allowed `sqs:SendMessage` in its identity policy, but the queue is in account B and the send is denied. What resource-side check is required?
constraints: The role policy names the correct queue ARN.
The queue is not public and should remain cross-account private.
No SCP or permissions boundary denies the action.

options.text: Add or correct the SQS queue policy in account B so it grants the intended account-A principal the required `SendMessage` action.
Remove the role policy because SQS queue policies alone are always sufficient for cross-account sends.
Make the queue anonymous so the source role's identity policy is not evaluated.
Use the account-B root access key in the producer because SQS cannot authorize roles.

feedback.Reason: Cross-account SQS access requires a resource policy in the queue account in addition to the source role's identity permission.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Amazon SQS supports queue policies that specify which principals may perform actions on a queue. The source role's identity policy and the queue policy must form a matching cross-account allow.
Details.scenarioApplication: The queue owner should grant only `sqs:SendMessage` to the intended role or account and retain the source role's exact queue permission.
Details.errorCorrection: Removing the identity policy or making the queue public abandons the two-sided boundary, and roles can be authorized by SQS.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A specific role principal is narrower than an entire source account, but the queue policy must match the actual cross-account principal representation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The source identity policy remains one side of the cross-account permission path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Anonymous access broadens the queue and is not a least-privilege repair.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SQS can authorize IAM roles; root keys are not required for producer access.

items.prompt: A notification publisher in another account has `sns:Publish` in its IAM policy, but Amazon SNS rejects the publish. The topic policy names a different account. What is the most direct correction?
constraints: The publisher uses the intended role session.
The topic ARN is correct.
The organization does not want to open the topic to all AWS principals.

options.text: Update the SNS topic policy to grant the intended source account or role the required publish action, while retaining the source identity allow.
Attach an IAM group to the SNS topic because resource policies cannot name accounts.
Remove all topic policies and use the root user in the publisher account.
Grant `sns:*` on every topic because publish permissions cannot be resource-scoped.

feedback.Reason: The topic account must grant the intended cross-account publisher through its SNS resource policy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SNS topic policies are resource-based policies that can grant principals in another account permission to publish. The caller's identity policy and the topic policy must both support the cross-account request.
Details.scenarioApplication: The topic owner should correct only the principal and `sns:Publish` statement needed for the publisher, keeping other topic actions closed.
Details.errorCorrection: IAM groups cannot be attached to an SNS topic, root use is not a cross-account authorization pattern, and wildcard SNS access is unnecessary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The policy can name a role or account depending on the intended lifecycle; naming an account is easier to operate but grants more potential principals.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SNS resource policies specify principals directly; IAM groups are not topic principals.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing the resource policy breaks the cross-account grant and root credentials are unsafe.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SNS publish can be scoped to a topic ARN and does not require all SNS actions on all topics.

items.prompt: A resource policy grants access to an IAM role ARN, but the request is made by a role session whose session policy denies the action. Why does the resource-policy allow not repair the failure?
constraints: The request uses temporary credentials for the assumed role.
The resource policy principal matches the intended role.
The session policy contains an explicit deny for the requested action.

options.text: An explicit deny in the applicable session authorization path overrides the resource-policy allow, so the session policy must be corrected or removed if approved.
Resource policies always override explicit denies in role sessions because they are attached to the resource.
The role session becomes anonymous when a resource policy names the role ARN.
The account root user must sign the request whenever a role ARN appears in a resource policy.

feedback.Reason: An explicit deny in an applicable policy layer overrides an allow from the resource policy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS policy evaluation gives explicit denies precedence over allows. A resource policy can be a granting surface, but it does not neutralize an explicit deny in another applicable session or identity policy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The authorization owner should inspect the session-policy issuance path and remove only the unjustified deny after confirming the intended role-session boundary.
Details.errorCorrection: Resource-based policy attachment does not create an allow-over-deny exception, and role sessions remain authenticated principals rather than anonymous users.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The diagnostic must account for whether the resource policy names the role ARN or a role session principal, but under the stated explicit deny the result remains denied.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Explicit denies override allows regardless of whether the allow comes from a resource policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A role session remains an authenticated assumed-role principal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A role ARN in a resource policy does not require root credentials.

items.prompt: An EC2 instance profile role trusts EC2, but the application receives `AccessDenied` for `s3:PutObject`. Which policy should be inspected after confirming role assumption succeeds?
constraints: The instance has obtained valid role credentials.
The role trust policy is known to work.
The application targets the expected bucket and object prefix.

options.text: Inspect the role's permissions policy and the bucket resource policy for the requested S3 action and object resource.
Edit the role trust policy to add `s3:PutObject` because trust policies grant data-plane actions.
Add the EC2 service principal to the object ARN so EC2 can write without role permissions.
Replace the instance profile with a root access key because trust succeeded but permissions do not matter.

feedback.Reason: Once role assumption succeeds, data-plane authorization is controlled by the role permissions and any applicable resource policy, not by the trust policy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A role trust policy establishes who or what may assume the role. The role permissions policy grants actions to the resulting session, and S3 can add a bucket policy as a resource-based authorization surface.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect should compare `s3:PutObject`, the object ARN, conditions, and bucket policy with the actual request.
Details.errorCorrection: Adding data actions to trust or replacing a working role with root credentials confuses authentication with authorization.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The role and bucket policies should be narrowed to the intended prefix and source role; broadening either is not necessary merely because the trust relationship is valid.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Trust policies do not grant data-plane actions after role assumption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A service principal is not a replacement for the role's S3 permission and resource policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The role already provides the intended workload identity; root credentials would add unrestricted risk.

items.prompt: A user in account A is trusted by a role in account B, but `AssumeRole` returns `AccessDenied`. The user's identity policy contains no `sts:AssumeRole` permission. Which correction is required?
constraints: The target role trust policy names the correct user or source account.
No SCP or explicit deny blocks the call.
The user should assume only the one target role.

options.text: Add a narrow `sts:AssumeRole` allow to the source user's or group policy for the exact target role ARN.
Add `sts:AssumeRole` to the target role permissions policy because trust and caller permission are the same statement.
Remove the target trust policy because a source identity allow can assume any role in another account.
Grant the source user the target account root password so the user can bypass STS.

feedback.Reason: Cross-account role assumption needs both target trust and source permission to call `sts:AssumeRole`.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The target role trust policy identifies who may assume the role, while the source principal's identity policy authorizes the STS API call. The target ARN should be resource-scoped.
Details.scenarioApplication: The source policy is the missing side, so adding the exact allow completes the intended role-assumption path without broadening trust.
Details.errorCorrection: The role permissions policy governs actions after assumption, and removing trust or distributing root credentials would break or weaken the design.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Both policies should be kept explicit and reviewed together because changing one side can change cross-account reachability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Role permissions control the assumed session's actions, not the source principal's permission to call AssumeRole.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The target role trust policy is required for cross-account assumption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root passwords are not an STS delegation mechanism and must not be shared.

items.prompt: A batch job fails with `ExpiredToken` only after a long idle period, then succeeds when restarted. Which fix preserves temporary credentials while addressing the failure?
constraints: The job uses an SDK credential provider for an assumed role.
The role policy is unchanged and allows the required action.
The job can refresh credentials before resuming work.

options.text: Ensure the provider refreshes the role session after idle time and before signing the resumed request.
Increase the role policy's action list because idle sessions lose permissions over time.
Disable STS expiration by placing the session token in an S3 bucket.
Replace the SDK provider with a root access key so idle credentials never expire.

feedback.Reason: The failure is a temporary-credential lifetime problem, so the workload needs a refreshable credential path rather than broader permissions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Temporary credentials have an expiration. SDK credential providers can obtain fresh role-session credentials and should refresh them before a request is signed after an idle period.
Details.scenarioApplication: The batch job can refresh on resume and retry the failed operation with a current session, preserving the short-lived role identity.
Details.errorCorrection: Idle time does not remove IAM permissions, and STS expiry cannot be disabled by storing a token; root keys are not a valid workaround.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The refresh path should be monitored and must not log secrets; increasing session duration may reduce refresh frequency but increases exposure time.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Credential expiration does not indicate a missing permission action.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Storing a token does not extend its expiration and creates unnecessary secret exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root keys are long-term unrestricted credentials and should not replace refreshable role credentials.

items.prompt: A team edited a customer managed policy to add `s3:PutObject`, but attached roles still receive `AccessDenied`. The new policy version exists, but it is not marked as the default version. What should be checked?
constraints: The policy is attached to the intended roles.
The new version is valid JSON and contains the required resource.
No other policy layer denies the request.

options.text: Set or verify the intended policy version as the default version so attached identities evaluate the updated document.
Create a second IAM group because attached managed policies never evaluate policy versions.
Delete the old version without changing the default marker because IAM reads every version at once.
Add the action to the root user because managed policy versions apply only to root.

feedback.Reason: Only the default version of a customer managed policy is used for authorization, so creating a version alone does not change effective permissions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM managed policies support multiple versions, but one version is designated as the default and is the version used when the policy is evaluated. Version changes should be tested and promoted deliberately.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should verify the default version and attachment, then test the role request; it should not broaden unrelated identities.
Details.errorCorrection: Groups do not solve an unapplied policy version, and IAM does not evaluate all versions together or attach them to root.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keeping prior versions can support rollback within policy limits, but the default marker remains the canonical effective version.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A second group does not promote the intended managed-policy version.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The policy must use the intended default version; deleting versions without that control can also remove rollback options.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Managed-policy versions apply to attached users, groups, and roles, not only root.

items.prompt: A user receives `AccessDenied` even though the expected read-only policy is attached to an IAM group. What membership fact should be checked first?
constraints: The policy is attached to the expected group.
The user is an IAM user, not a role session.
No explicit deny or boundary is involved.

options.text: Verify that the exact IAM user is a member of the group in the account where the request is made.
Attach the group to the user's role because IAM users inherit group membership through every role.
Add the policy to root because group policies are evaluated only for root sessions.
Rename the group to match the user's name because IAM authorizes membership by display-name similarity.

feedback.Reason: IAM group policies apply to IAM users who are members of that group; membership is an explicit authorization relationship.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM groups collect users for policy assignment. A user must be added to the group, and group policies do not automatically apply to arbitrary roles or identities with similar names.
Details.scenarioApplication: The administrator should inspect membership in the correct account and then re-evaluate the user's exact principal and policy context.
Details.errorCorrection: Groups are not attached to roles, root does not inherit group policies, and names do not create membership.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Group membership is convenient for shared user permissions, but workforce-scale access may be better centralized through IAM Identity Center rather than many IAM users.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: IAM groups contain users and are not attached to roles.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root is not an ordinary IAM group member and should not be used for this diagnostic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM evaluates explicit membership, not display-name similarity.

items.prompt: A team updated a customer managed policy, but an IAM role still lacks the new permission. The policy is attached to a group containing users, not to the role. What is the likely defect?
constraints: The request is made by the IAM role.
The policy document contains the correct allow.
No resource policy or organization control changes the result.

options.text: Attach the policy to the intended role or attach an equivalent managed policy through the role's canonical authorization path.
Add the role to the IAM group because roles inherit all group-user policies.
Attach the policy to root because every IAM identity reads root policies.
Change the policy's group name to the role name because attachment is inferred from names.

feedback.Reason: An identity-based policy must be attached to the principal type that makes the request; IAM groups contain users and do not grant their policies to roles.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM managed policies can attach to users, groups, or roles as supported. A role session evaluates policies attached to the role and other applicable sources, not policies attached to an unrelated user group.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should attach the reviewed policy to the role or use a role-specific managed policy, then verify the role session's effective permissions.
Details.errorCorrection: Role-group membership and name matching are not IAM inheritance mechanisms, and root policies are not a shared identity policy source.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The attachment change should be reviewed for role blast radius; attaching a broad existing policy to the role may be less safe than creating a scoped role policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: IAM groups contain users; roles do not inherit group policies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root is not a policy inheritance layer for IAM roles.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Policy attachment is explicit and is not inferred from names.

items.prompt: A resource policy names `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Deploy`, but the actual role is `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/team/Deploy`. Why might the request still be denied?
constraints: The policy is intended to name one exact role.
The role path is part of its ARN.
No other resource or identity policy grants access.

options.text: The resource policy principal ARN omits the role path, so it does not match the actual role principal; correct the ARN if that role is intended.
Role paths are comments and never participate in IAM ARN matching.
Add the role's password to the policy because paths are validated through passwords.
Use the root ARN as a wildcard replacement for every role path.

feedback.Reason: IAM role paths are part of role ARNs, so an ARN without the actual path may not match the intended role.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM ARNs identify roles using the path and role name. Resource policies and identity policies that use a role ARN must match the principal and resource identifiers used by the request.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should confirm the actual ARN and correct only the resource-policy principal if the `team/Deploy` role is the intended caller.
Details.errorCorrection: Role paths are not comments, and passwords or root ARNs are not safe or valid substitutes for principal matching.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A carefully scoped principal ARN improves least privilege; wildcarding paths can grant more roles than intended.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The role path is part of the ARN and can affect principal matching.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM role passwords are not used to match resource-policy principals.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A root ARN is not a wildcard for every role and would not express the intended role boundary.

items.prompt: A policy uses `Allow` with `NotAction` and a wildcard resource for a role intended to manage only one service. Which diagnostic concern should be raised?
constraints: The policy author intended a narrow service boundary.
The role is used by a production workload.
No explicit deny limits the resulting allow.

options.text: Review and replace the broad `NotAction` pattern with an explicit allow list, because it can grant every action except the listed exclusions.
Keep it because `NotAction` always means no action is allowed when `Resource` is `*`.
Add a root access key so the broad policy is unnecessary at runtime.
Move the `NotAction` statement into a password policy because password rules narrow service actions.

feedback.Reason: An Allow statement with `NotAction` can be broader than its excluded actions suggest, especially with a wildcard resource.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: `NotAction` matches every action except those specified, subject to the policy context and resource support. In an Allow statement it can grant broad permissions and is difficult to reason about as services evolve.
Details.scenarioApplication: The role should use explicit actions and resource scopes for the intended service rather than relying on a negative allow pattern.
Details.errorCorrection: `NotAction` does not mean no action, and password policies or root keys do not narrow an authorization statement.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Negative statements can have valid deny use cases, but an allow-based exclusion list needs strong review because new actions may become included unintentionally.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: In an Allow statement, `NotAction` means all actions except the listed exclusions, not no actions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root credentials do not make an overbroad policy safer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Password policies govern passwords and do not contain service-action authorization.

items.prompt: A deny statement uses `NotResource` to block deletion of two production buckets. What review is needed before treating it as a complete protection?
constraints: The statement is intended to protect only production data.
The account contains additional buckets that must not be deleted by the role.
The statement is the only deletion safeguard in the role policy.

options.text: Review the negative resource scope carefully; `NotResource` can deny the action on every resource except the listed exclusions and may not express the intended allow boundary.
Assume `NotResource` always means only the two listed buckets are affected.
Remove all explicit denies because IAM cannot evaluate resource exclusions.
Use the root user to delete nonproduction buckets because deny statements never apply to root.

feedback.Reason: `NotResource` matches every resource except those listed, so a deny can affect more resources than the author expects.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The `NotResource` element specifies resources that do not match the statement; in a Deny, the statement can deny the action for all other matching resources. The effect must be evaluated with the action and other conditions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should use explicit resource allows or a carefully reviewed deny boundary that covers the complete deletion contract, not assume the exclusions define the only affected resources.
Details.errorCorrection: `NotResource` does not mean only the listed resources, and removing denies or relying on root creates unsafe gaps.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Negative resource patterns can protect broad sets but are easy to misread and may affect future resources; explicit resource lists or service guardrails may be clearer.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The listed resources are the exclusions from the match, not the only resources affected by the deny.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Explicit denies remain useful, but this one must be reviewed for correct scope.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root can be affected by organization controls and should not be used to bypass deletion safeguards.

items.prompt: An IAM allow requires a request tag through a `Null` condition, but an SDK call without that tag is denied. What should the architect inspect?
constraints: The policy condition is intentionally part of the security boundary.
The request does not include the required tag key.
No other policy grants the action.

options.text: Inspect the `Null` condition semantics and the request context; a missing key can make the allow condition fail.
Add the action to the role trust policy because condition keys authenticate the caller before IAM evaluates permissions.
Disable all conditions because conditions are advisory metadata only.
Use a root access key because root requests never carry request context.

feedback.Reason: Conditions are part of the authorization match; a missing request context value can prevent an allow from applying.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The `Null` condition operator tests whether a condition key is absent or present. If an allow requires the key to be present, a request that omits it does not satisfy the statement.
Details.scenarioApplication: The SDK must supply the required tag or the policy must be intentionally redesigned; the team should not bypass the condition with a broad allow.
Details.errorCorrection: Trust policies and request conditions solve different stages, and conditions are enforced authorization logic rather than comments.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Request-tag controls require all legitimate clients to send the context consistently and may need separate create and update permissions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Trust policies do not repair a condition mismatch in a permissions policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Conditions are evaluated by AWS and can be a critical least-privilege control.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root credentials are not a safe way to bypass request-context controls.

items.prompt: A policy allows access when `aws:PrincipalTag/Team` equals `Finance`. The role session is denied because the role has no `Team` tag. Which correction preserves the ABAC boundary?
constraints: The policy intentionally uses the principal tag as the authorization attribute.
The role is managed by a platform team.
The team can control which tags are allowed on the role.

options.text: Apply and govern the required `Team=Finance` principal tag only if the role is approved for that team, then retest the policy context.
Replace the condition with `*` because tags are not evaluated for role sessions.
Add the tag to the S3 bucket only because principal tags are read from resources.
Give the role administrator access so it can impersonate the Finance team without a tag.

feedback.Reason: The policy is intentionally attribute-based, so the principal must have the required governed attribute for the allow to match.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The `aws:PrincipalTag` global condition key evaluates tags attached to the principal. The tag value becomes part of authorization context and must be protected from unauthorized changes.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team should tag only an approved Finance role and verify the tag lifecycle; if the role is not Finance, the correct result is denial.
Details.errorCorrection: Replacing the condition with a wildcard or administrator permission defeats ABAC, and resource tags are a different context source.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: ABAC reduces policy duplication but makes tag governance part of the security boundary; tag mutation permissions must be tightly controlled.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Role sessions can be evaluated with principal tags, and removing the condition broadens access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Principal tags are attributes of the identity, not tags on the target resource.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Administrator access bypasses the intended team attribute and is not a safe diagnostic fix.

items.prompt: An S3 bucket policy allows a role only when `aws:SourceVpce` equals the company's interface endpoint. The role succeeds from the VPC but fails from a public network. What does the failure indicate?
constraints: The role identity policy allows the object action.
The public request does not traverse the specified VPC endpoint.
The bucket is intentionally private to endpoint traffic.

options.text: The resource-policy condition is working as designed; the request must use the approved VPC endpoint or the policy must be deliberately changed.
Add administrator access because SourceVpce conditions are ignored outside the VPC.
Change the role trust policy to include the endpoint ID because trust policies control network origin.
Make the bucket public so the endpoint condition no longer evaluates.

feedback.Reason: A `aws:SourceVpce` condition restricts the resource-policy allow to requests that arrive through the specified VPC endpoint.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Global condition keys can evaluate network context supplied with a request. `aws:SourceVpce` can be used to restrict supported resource access to a particular VPC endpoint.
Details.scenarioApplication: The public request is correctly denied under the stated private-access design; the application or operator must use the endpoint path rather than bypassing the condition.
Details.errorCorrection: Administrator access and role trust do not override a resource-policy network condition, and public access would remove the intended boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Endpoint-based restrictions require complete routing and DNS design; emergency paths should be explicit rather than silently broadening the bucket policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Broad permissions do not make a request satisfy a resource-policy condition and would enlarge access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Role trust controls assumption, not the network origin condition on a resource request.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public access abandons the endpoint-only security boundary.

items.prompt: An S3 bucket has an allow for the correct role but a global deny when `aws:SecureTransport` is false. A legacy client uses plain HTTP and receives `AccessDenied`. What is the correct diagnosis?
constraints: The role identity policy and bucket allow match the object.
The request is genuinely unsigned or otherwise valid for the service except for transport security.
The bucket owner intends to require TLS.

options.text: The explicit transport-security deny overrides the allow; update the client to use HTTPS rather than removing the deny.
Add more role permissions because explicit denies are ignored when an allow matches.
Change the root MFA setting because SecureTransport is an authentication factor.
Make the bucket public so the client can use HTTP without IAM evaluation.

feedback.Reason: An explicit deny based on `aws:SecureTransport` overrides the identity and resource allows, so the client must satisfy the transport requirement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The `aws:SecureTransport` global condition key can be used to deny requests that are not sent over TLS. Explicit denies take precedence over matching allows.
Details.scenarioApplication: The legacy client should be upgraded or configured for HTTPS; removing the deny would weaken protection for every principal accessing the bucket.
Details.errorCorrection: Additional permissions cannot override an explicit deny, and MFA or public access is unrelated to the transport control.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A migration may require a controlled client upgrade path, but any exception should be narrowly scoped and time-bounded rather than deleting the bucket-wide safeguard.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Explicit denies override allows and cannot be fixed by adding more actions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: SecureTransport evaluates network protocol, not MFA configuration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public access would remove the intended authorization and transport boundary.

items.prompt: An IAM user can perform routine reads but receives `AccessDenied` for `iam:CreateAccessKey` because the policy requires MFA. The CLI request used an access key without an MFA-authenticated session. What should change?
constraints: The MFA condition is intentional for this sensitive action.
The user has an approved MFA device.
The team must not remove the condition just to make the CLI call succeed.

options.text: Use an MFA-authenticated request or redesign the workflow around a role/federated session that supplies the required context.
Add `iam:CreateAccessKey` to an unconditional allow so the access key itself proves MFA.
Put the MFA code in the access-key ID so IAM can infer that the user used MFA.
Use the root user's access key because root access keys always carry MFA context.

feedback.Reason: The request lacks the authentication context required by the sensitive-action condition, so the correct fix is to use an MFA-capable session or approved workflow.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` evaluates whether the request context includes MFA for supported credential flows. An ordinary long-term access-key request does not automatically satisfy a human MFA requirement.
Details.scenarioApplication: The user should authenticate through the permitted MFA path or assume a role designed for the operation, while the policy condition remains in force.
Details.errorCorrection: An access-key identifier and a caller-supplied code are not trusted MFA context, and root access keys are not an MFA workflow.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The organization should distinguish human self-service from machine automation so MFA conditions do not create unsafe workarounds or break workload roles.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An unconditional allow removes the intended MFA control and does not make the access key prove MFA.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Access-key identifiers are not authenticated MFA evidence and cannot be modified for this purpose.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root access keys are long-term unrestricted credentials and do not automatically carry MFA context.

items.prompt: IAM Access Analyzer reports a security warning that a policy grants access to an overly broad resource. The application needs only one queue. What is the best remediation?
constraints: The policy is still in review.
The application has a stable queue ARN.
The team wants to preserve the required send action.

options.text: Replace the broad resource with the exact queue ARN, then revalidate and test the intended request.
Ignore the warning because policy validation warnings are always false positives.
Grant administrator access so the warning no longer matters at runtime.
Delete the queue so no policy can grant access to it.

feedback.Reason: The stable queue ARN allows the policy to express the application's actual least-privilege resource boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM Access Analyzer policy validation can surface security warnings and recommendations during policy authoring. The author should address relevant breadth findings while confirming the policy still satisfies the workload contract.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team can narrow the resource to the one queue, rerun validation, and use the policy simulator or integration test for the send operation.
Details.errorCorrection: Warnings should be evaluated, not dismissed categorically, and administrator access or deletion is not a policy remediation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the queue set is dynamic, the team may need a carefully scoped naming or tag strategy, but a wildcard should not be retained merely for convenience.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A warning about excessive resource scope is directly relevant to least privilege and should be reviewed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Administrator access increases risk and does not resolve the broad policy finding.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting the resource is destructive and unrelated to correcting the authorization scope.

items.prompt: IAM Access Analyzer reports that an S3 bucket policy grants access to an external AWS account. The business owner expected only an internal role to access the bucket. What should happen first?
constraints: The external account is not part of the approved data-sharing contract.
The finding identifies a resource-policy exposure.
The team can change the bucket policy after confirming the intended principal.

options.text: Review the bucket policy principal and remove or narrow the external allow after confirming that no approved integration depends on it.
Ignore the finding because Access Analyzer findings are authorization grants, not exposure evidence.
Make the bucket public so the external account is no longer a special case.
Rotate the root password because resource policies are stored in root credentials.

feedback.Reason: The finding is evidence that a resource policy permits external access and should be reconciled with the approved sharing contract.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM Access Analyzer analyzes resource policies for access from outside the zone of trust and produces findings that help owners identify unintended external access.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner should verify the principal, required action, and business dependency, then remove or scope the external statement if it is not approved.
Details.errorCorrection: Ignoring an unexpected external grant or making the resource public increases exposure; root credentials are unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Some external integrations are intentional, so remediation must distinguish approved sharing from accidental exposure rather than deleting every cross-account policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An external-access finding is specifically useful evidence about a resource-policy grant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public access is broader than the reported external account and violates least privilege.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Resource policy exposure is not controlled by the root password.

items.prompt: The IAM policy simulator reports an allow, but the production request is denied by a condition on `aws:SourceIp`. What limitation should the team consider?
constraints: The simulator test omitted the actual source IP context.
The production policy condition is active.
The team can rerun the simulation with representative context values.

options.text: Supply the relevant request context to the simulation and verify the actual network path; a simulation with missing context may not reproduce the production condition.
Trust the simulator unconditionally because it automatically knows the production source IP.
Remove the condition because policy simulators cannot evaluate any conditions.
Use the root user to make the production request because root sessions have no source IP.

feedback.Reason: Policy simulation depends on the principal, action, resource, and supplied context; omitted context can produce a result that differs from production.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The IAM policy simulator can test context keys and request parameters, but the operator must provide values that represent the request being evaluated. It is a what-if tool, not a live network observer.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should simulate the production source IP or test the real path, then retain the condition if it is the intended boundary.
Details.errorCorrection: The simulator does not automatically infer every production context value, and deleting a network condition or using root would weaken security.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Context-dependent authorization needs test cases for each approved network path, including endpoint and operational paths.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The simulator needs relevant context input and is not automatically connected to production network state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The simulator supports condition testing; a condition mismatch is not a reason to remove a valid control.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root requests still have network context and root use is not a safe bypass.

items.prompt: An incident responder cannot find an S3 `GetObject` call in the CloudTrail management-event trail. The responder needs object-level caller evidence. What should be checked?
constraints: The bucket object request may be a data event.
The current trail logs management events only.
The team needs future forensic visibility rather than a policy change.

options.text: Configure CloudTrail data-event logging for the relevant S3 bucket or object scope, then retain and monitor those events.
Grant the incident responder administrator access because CloudTrail management events include every object read automatically.
Store the object's caller identity in the S3 object key so CloudTrail can infer it later.
Use the root MFA device serial number as a substitute for an absent data event.

feedback.Reason: S3 object operations are data events and require appropriate CloudTrail data-event configuration for object-level audit visibility.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudTrail separates management events from data events. Data-event logging can be configured for supported resource types such as S3 objects and provides detailed object-level API activity for the selected scope.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should enable the needed S3 data events for future evidence and define retention and cost controls; missing historical events cannot be reconstructed by changing IAM permissions.
Details.errorCorrection: Administrator access does not make an existing trail record data events, and object names or MFA serials are not audit substitutes.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Data events increase logging volume and cost, so the selector should be scoped to sensitive buckets or prefixes and reviewed with the threat model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Management-event visibility is a trail configuration issue, not a responder permission issue.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Object naming does not cause CloudTrail to record the caller identity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An MFA serial cannot replace an absent object-level CloudTrail event.

items.prompt: An analyst searches CloudTrail in `eu-west-1` for an IAM role change made in `us-east-1` and finds nothing. What should be verified?
constraints: The change was a regional service event or was recorded in the event's source Region.
The analyst has access to the trail's destination.
The request identity is not the current question.

options.text: Search the event Region and the trail's centralized destination, because CloudTrail events carry a Region and regional coverage must be configured appropriately.
Change the IAM policy to grant CloudTrail access in all Regions; event storage is independent of trail configuration.
Search only the account root user's activity because IAM changes are always root events.
Delete the `us-east-1` trail so events are copied into `eu-west-1` automatically.

feedback.Reason: CloudTrail event discovery depends on the event Region and the trail or event-data configuration, not merely the analyst's current console Region.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudTrail events include the AWS Region where the event occurred, and trails can be configured for Regions and delivered to a destination. A regional search can miss events recorded elsewhere.
Details.scenarioApplication: The analyst should query the correct event Region and centralized S3 or CloudTrail Lake destination while preserving the IAM permissions used to read the logs.
Details.errorCorrection: Granting CloudTrail permissions cannot create an event that was not selected or searched, and IAM changes are not automatically root events.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A multi-Region trail or centralized event store improves coverage but adds configuration and cost that should be validated as part of the audit design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Viewer permissions do not determine whether a trail recorded an event or which Region contains it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM changes can be made by many principals and are not inherently root events.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting a trail is destructive and does not copy prior events to another Region.

items.prompt: A user assigned a permission set is denied in one account. An administrator manually edited the IAM role created by IAM Identity Center, but the permission set still lacks the action. Where should the canonical fix be made?
constraints: The user and group assignment are correct.
The generated role is managed by IAM Identity Center.
The action is required by the approved permission set contract.

options.text: Update the permission set in IAM Identity Center and allow it to reconcile the managed role, then verify propagation.
Continue adding account-local edits to the generated role because Identity Center never overwrites them.
Add the action to the user's root account policy because permission sets inherit root permissions.
Create a second IAM user in the account so the user can bypass the permission set role.

feedback.Reason: The permission set is the source of truth for the IAM Identity Center-controlled role and should be updated through its owning control plane.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM Identity Center creates and manages roles in target accounts from permission sets. Updating the permission set lets Identity Center propagate the policy change consistently to the assignment.
Details.scenarioApplication: The administrator should add only the approved action to the permission set, wait for reconciliation, and retest the user's role session.
Details.errorCorrection: Direct edits to generated roles create drift and may be overwritten; root policies and account-local IAM users do not repair the central assignment.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If an account-specific exception is real, it should be modeled explicitly as a separate permission set or architecture decision rather than hidden in generated-role edits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Generated-role edits are not the canonical ownership path and can drift or be overwritten.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root permissions are not inherited by Identity Center permission sets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A second IAM user bypasses the workforce control and creates unnecessary lifecycle work.

items.prompt: A SAML-federated user can authenticate to the IdP but cannot obtain an AWS console session because the assertion requests a role ARN that does not exist in the account. What should be checked?
constraints: The SAML assertion is signed and accepted by AWS.
The role ARN in the assertion is account-qualified.
The user should receive only the approved role.

options.text: Correct the IdP role attribute to reference an existing IAM role and ensure that role trusts the SAML provider.
Add the role ARN as an S3 object so the SAML provider can discover it.
Create a root user with the same role name so SAML can fall back to root.
Grant the IdP administrator permission to pass any role without changing the assertion.

feedback.Reason: SAML federation must identify a real IAM role that trusts the SAML provider; authentication alone does not create the requested role.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS SAML federation uses assertion attributes to identify the roles the federated user may assume. The IAM role must exist and its trust policy must allow the SAML provider principal.
Details.scenarioApplication: The IdP administrator should correct the account-qualified role attribute and the AWS administrator should verify the role trust and permissions independently.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 objects and root identities are not SAML role discovery fallbacks, and broad PassRole access does not create or authenticate a role session.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The IdP role mapping should be maintained from an approved role catalogue so decommissioned or privileged roles do not remain selectable.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SAML role attributes refer to IAM roles, not S3 objects.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root users do not substitute for IAM roles in SAML federation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: PassRole is unrelated to the user's SAML role assertion and would broaden delegation.

items.prompt: CloudTrail shows many changes made by the same assumed role, but operations cannot link them to individual pipeline runs. Which change improves attribution without changing permissions?
constraints: The same role is intentionally shared by several approved automation systems.
Each system can supply a unique nonsecret run identifier.
CloudTrail is already logging the management events.

options.text: Use unique meaningful role session names or source identities for each run and correlate them with the deployment records.
Use one generic session name for every run so all events appear under one identity.
Place the pipeline secret in the session name so only security can read the audit trail.
Replace the role with one shared root access key so all automation has one stable credential.

feedback.Reason: Unique nonsecret session attribution improves correlation of assumed-role activity without expanding the role's permissions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: STS role sessions support session naming and source identity context that can be surfaced in audit records. Those values help correlate a role session with an originating workload or run.
Details.scenarioApplication: Each pipeline uses a stable run identifier, and the operations team maps that identifier to the deployment record when reviewing CloudTrail.
Details.errorCorrection: Generic names hide provenance, secrets must not be placed in log-visible identifiers, and root keys reduce rather than improve audit separation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Attribution metadata is not authentication or authorization; the role still needs least-privilege permissions and CloudTrail retention.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A generic name makes events harder to distinguish across runs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Secrets must not be exposed in session names or audit records.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A shared root key creates a high-impact long-term secret and loses useful session context.

items.prompt: An employee was disabled in the external IdP, but an existing IAM Identity Center portal session still accesses an AWS account. What should the incident team examine?
constraints: The organization uses an external IdP as the Identity Center identity source.
SCIM synchronization reports the user as disabled.
The incident response plan includes session revocation and assignment checks.

options.text: Check active portal and AWS-account sessions, SCIM status, and account assignments, then apply the documented revocation procedure.
Assume IdP disable immediately terminates every already-issued AWS session without verification.
Rotate the account root password because workforce sessions are derived from root credentials.
Delete all permission sets so no session can continue, regardless of other employees.

feedback.Reason: Workforce offboarding requires checking both downstream provisioning and already-issued sessions; an IdP state change is not evidence that every session has ended.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM Identity Center uses the identity source for workforce lifecycle and account assignments for authorization. Sessions already issued to a user may have their own lifetime and revocation behavior that must be handled by the operational procedure.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should revoke or expire the active sessions as supported, verify the user has no remaining assignments, and retain SCIM as the authoritative lifecycle path.
Details.errorCorrection: Assuming immediate termination can leave an active session, and deleting shared permission sets would disrupt unrelated users.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Session revocation and propagation timing should be tested before an incident; shorter sessions reduce the window but do not replace offboarding checks.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Synchronization and session behavior must be verified; disabling the source identity is not the same as proving every session ended.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root credentials are not the source of workforce sessions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting permission sets is destructive and affects other authorized users.

items.prompt: An account root user in a member account receives an organization-level denial for an action that an SCP does not allow. Which conclusion is correct?
constraints: The account is a member account in an AWS Organization with applicable SCPs.
The SCP is an allow-list maximum that omits the requested action.
No other policy issue is being considered.

options.text: The SCP limits the member account's root user as part of the account's maximum permissions, so the organization administrator must change the guardrail if the action is approved.
The root user always bypasses SCPs, so the denial proves the root password is wrong.
Add the action to an IAM group because root users inherit group policies.
Create an access key for the root user because SCPs apply only to console sessions.

feedback.Reason: AWS Organizations SCPs can limit permissions for member-account root users; root is not an automatic organizational-policy bypass.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SCPs define the maximum permissions available to IAM users and roles within member accounts and can also affect the member account root user. They do not grant permissions by themselves.
Details.scenarioApplication: The organization administrator must review the SCP if the action is approved; changing an in-account IAM policy or root credential cannot expand beyond the SCP maximum.
Details.errorCorrection: Root does not bypass an SCP, does not inherit group policies, and should not receive an access key to evade a guardrail.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Changing an SCP can affect many principals, so the organization-level blast radius and exception design must be reviewed before modification.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SCPs can limit member-account root users, so the denial is not proof of a bad password.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root users are not IAM group members.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SCP evaluation is not limited to console sessions, and root access keys are unsafe.

items.prompt: An S3 bucket policy grants a role ARN access, but a role session has an explicit deny in its permissions boundary. Which diagnostic rule should guide the investigation?
constraints: The role ARN is the intended principal.
The boundary applies to the role.
No other policy can grant a permission beyond the boundary under the stated request path.

options.text: Inspect the boundary and other maximum layers; the resource-policy allow does not eliminate an applicable explicit deny or maximum restriction.
Assume the role ARN in a resource policy always bypasses the role's boundary.
Replace the role session with root because boundaries apply only to users.
Remove the bucket policy because resource policies can never authorize role sessions.

feedback.Reason: A matching resource-policy allow is only one part of effective authorization; applicable boundaries and explicit denies still constrain the role session.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Permissions boundaries limit identity-based grants for users and roles, and explicit denies override allows. The exact interaction depends on whether the resource policy names a role ARN or role session principal, but an explicit boundary deny remains effective.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect should inspect and correct the boundary only if the action is approved; changing the bucket policy alone cannot remove the boundary restriction.
Details.errorCorrection: Role ARN resource policies are not universal bypasses, root is not a diagnostic substitute, and resource policies can authorize role sessions in supported services.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The policy evaluator must preserve the principal form and all maximum layers rather than applying a simplified union rule to every role request.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A role ARN resource-policy allow does not automatically bypass an applicable explicit boundary deny.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Permissions boundaries can apply to roles, and root should not replace the workload identity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Resource policies can authorize role sessions; the issue is the additional boundary layer.

items.prompt: A delegated team can create IAM roles with a permissions boundary, but a new role has no access even though its identity policy allows S3 reads. The boundary omits `s3:GetObject`. What should the administrator explain?
constraints: The boundary is attached to the role.
The identity policy and object ARN are otherwise correct.
The delegated team cannot remove the boundary without central approval.

options.text: The boundary sets the role's maximum permissions, so the central boundary must allow the approved S3 action before the role policy can be effective.
The boundary grants every action not listed, so the identity policy should be deleted.
Remove the boundary from all roles because boundaries never apply to newly created roles.
Give the delegated team root credentials so it can bypass the boundary.

feedback.Reason: The permissions boundary limits what a newly created role can receive from its identity policy, so an omitted action remains unavailable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A permissions boundary is a managed policy that defines the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can have. It does not grant permissions, and the identity policy and boundary must both allow the action.
Details.scenarioApplication: The central team should approve and update the boundary only if the delegated role's contract requires the S3 read; otherwise the denial is the intended guardrail.
Details.errorCorrection: A boundary does not grant unlisted actions, and removing it or using root would defeat delegated-administration containment.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central boundaries reduce the blast radius of delegated role creation but must be versioned and tested as a shared control.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A boundary is a maximum allow set, not a negative exclusion that grants every unlisted action.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Boundaries apply to roles when attached, including newly created roles.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root credentials should not be distributed to bypass a central authorization guardrail.

items.prompt: A managed policy was updated to remove `s3:DeleteObject`, but a role still appears able to delete objects. The role also has an inline policy with that action. What should the review conclude?
constraints: The managed policy's new default version is active.
The inline policy is attached directly to the role.
No explicit deny was added elsewhere.

options.text: The inline policy remains an independent identity-based allow, so it must be removed or narrowed if the role should no longer delete objects.
Changing the managed policy automatically deletes every inline policy attached to the role.
Add a second managed policy with `Deny` on every S3 action because inline policies cannot be inspected.
Use the root user to delete the inline policy because role policies are immutable.

feedback.Reason: Managed and inline identity policies are separate applicable policy sources; updating one does not remove an allow in the other.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM evaluates policies attached to the identity, including managed and inline policies. A managed-policy version change affects that managed policy only, while an inline policy remains attached directly to the role until changed or removed.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should inventory both policy types, remove the delete action from the inline policy if approved, and retest the effective role permissions.
Details.errorCorrection: Policy changes do not mutate unrelated inline policies, and adding broad denies or using root is not the smallest correction.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Inline policies can express a tight one-to-one relationship but are harder to discover across identities; the team should choose a canonical ownership path and audit duplicates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Managed policy versions do not delete or rewrite unrelated inline policies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A broad deny is more disruptive than removing the specific inline allow and is not required to diagnose the source.
